items.title: David Silver and Lasse Espeholt of Ineffable Intelligence: A Superlearner for the Age of Experience
items.content: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:32 Collectively, you know, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head. We somehow started out knowing nothing at all and somehow discovered, like, everything that humans know today was, like, this process of collective discovery, like, of of languages and technology and science and mathematics and all the rest of it. Know, everything we learned, we discovered it for ourselves. And that's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI. And so to me, that is the essence of what it will take to get to superintelligence, like a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever. Speaker 2 | 00:49 - 01:10 I'm thrilled to have Dave Silver and Lesae Espeholt with us, two of the co founders of ineffable intelligence. Great name, by the way. Fun fact, Dave, you were the first person I cold emailed to come on training data when we started the show 100 ish episodes ago. And it feels like a full circle moment to finally have you on the show. So thank you for joining us. Speaker 1 | 01:11 - 01:11 Thank you. Speaker 2 | 01:12 - 01:43 Dave, let's start with you. Your 2009 PhD was on reinforcement learning applied to the devilishly difficult game of Go. You demonstrated for the world for the first time that superhuman in one domain machine intelligence was possible. And I think you were really the figure that inspired the entire current generation of reinforcement learning and deep learning researchers. And so thank you for your contributions to where the field is. Speaker 2 | 01:44 - 01:57 I'm curious, thinking back to that point in time, what did you learn? What did you have conviction on? And what has remained the same and what has changed as AI has changed over the last five years or so? Speaker 1 | 01:57 - 02:47 Yeah. Thank you, and pleasure to be here, and I'm glad I finally made it after these 100 episodes. It's a pleasure to be here. So I suppose I always had this conviction starting my PhD and going into the game of Go that the right approach to solve AI was through learning from experience, through systems that discovered things for themselves, that were learning through reinforcement learning to get better and better and better, and that that would be the thing which would lead to the emergence of intelligence and ultimately superintelligence. And so I suppose we were able to show that in the game of Go, but it's a conviction that has held true throughout my career, and here we are now applying that conviction, ineffable, trying to show that indeed superintelligence can emerge all the way through systems that learn from experience. Speaker 1 | 02:48 - 03:39 And in terms of things which are different, although we are not pursuing the human data path that the LLM world has pursued, I do think there's lots of interesting lessons to learn from that. In particular, it was definitely a surprise to me how a system that was trained on a massive amount of data could then be very quickly fine tuned on a very small amount of data to completely change its behavior. That was something which I think was something which changed my mindset in terms of just suggesting that if you get things at the right scale, that a lot of things which seem incredibly hard or they might be very slow, that once you've kind of experienced enough data, that after that, the things that were slow can become very fast. I think that's a lesson that wasn't obvious to me in advance until it happened. Speaker 2 | 03:39 - 03:56 Okay, we're going to come back to that later. You could have run this program inside DeepMind where could have probably had more access to compute than just about anybody. You decided the right thing to do was to start a new lab. Why'd you do that? Speaker 1 | 03:57 - 04:31 Yeah. So look, first of all, I had a fantastic time at DeepMind. items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.content: At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share…

items.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.content: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale  StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student  The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance  Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor  In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess,…

items.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. items.title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
items.content: OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today. One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety . Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week. The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment , rather than how many restrictions you impose. Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.dev Adding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev today Joseph Kim , Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.” Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents. He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.” The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability . “In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Fi…

items.title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
items.content: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack , and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding , or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is . Their substack — or at least Owl Posting ’s 1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI. So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules. 2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing. It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint , blog , and open dataset . We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned! We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this. Enjoy! items.title: Dyna-2: General Purpose Physical Agents with Hour-Long Autonomy — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
items.content: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month! This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube . Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2 , a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude . They have now followed up the model with a physical robot agent, Dyna-2.1 , that has to be seen to be believed: In his talk at AIE this year, Jason talked about how the real challenge for robotics in the real world is reliable, long-horizon autonomy , and how Dyna got its models to a 99.4% success rate folding restaurant napkins for 24 hours straight, including recovering after it pulled over the whole stack. From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung , Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers. We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna’s million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of r…
items.summary: Our first robotics pod with Dyna’s Chief Scientist on their big bet on World Action Models & the Next Frontier of Physical AI

items.title: [AINews] Meta Muse Wonder & Wonder Full: MSL’s Claude 5.5-tier Frontier Model
items.content: We have been coveringe MSL’s 14 month journey to becoming a frontier lab , but only today did the final ball drop: Meta’s Muse Wonder to match Spark and Glimmer , the way that OpenAI has Sol/Terra/Luna and Anthropic has Opus/Sonnet/Haiku. Interestingly, while Muse doesn’t claim a specific size, Muse Wonder Full does beat Fable and Astra on some benchmarks, and with various degrees of posttraining it is a little unclear if Wonder is more of a Fable/Astra class model or not. We have included a full breakdown of launch details below. AI News for 10/10/2026-10/12/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Meta launches Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full What happened Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) shipped Muse Wonder (codename “Watermelon” 🍉), its second-generation model family. Third-party evals put it near the frontier, roughly 14 months after the lab was founded. The run-up. Hours before launch, insiders posted watermelon teasers: @rpnickson (”It is a BIG watermelon…”), @alexandr_wang , @finkd (”Muse ordered me 🍉”) and @EdwardSun0909 . @kimmonismus relayed leaked pricing from @synthwavedd: $4/M input, $20/M output, a 1M context window, and the max-reasoning “Wonder Full” tier exclusive to MuseCode Power/Maximum Usage plans. Two models. @finkd announced the family. He explained that Muse Spark was MSL’s first family and Wonder is “a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier.” The two releases are Muse Wonder (fast frontier) and Muse Wonder Full (the full model). Availability is split ( @AIatMeta , Newsroom ): Wonder is available via the Meta Model API and Muse Code. Full is available only to Muse Code subscribers. Wonder wi…

items.title: 10 Takeaways from Q3
items.content: AI, China, defense, national security, supply chains, the Protestant roots of Kim Il-sung’s Messiah complex , the lethality of hydrofluoric acid, and horseback archery in Kyrgyzstan. It’s been a productive Q3. Here are some of the things we learned and why we think they matter. The ChinaTalk team is growing! We’ve welcomed Quinn Ennis , our newest full-time analyst, and Michael Palmer , who has been doing great work behind the scenes on video and audio! China and AI What does Liang Wenfeng actually believe? The DeepSeek Thesis reconstructs DeepSeek’s strategy from leaked minutes of a four-hour meeting between Liang Wenfeng and investors. For Liang, general intelligence is the only problem worth solving — products can wait, because “once truly generalized and convincingly superior intelligence arrives, creating to-C and to-B products will be trivial.” Why it matters: This is a rare window into the worldview of one of the most important people in Chinese AI. Liang is all-in on AGI rather than diverting focus toward commercializing current AI capabilities, and he’s betting that open models and Chinese chips can get him there. Why are Chinese AI researchers so skeptical of American AI safety? In How Chinese AI Radicalizes , Irene traces an unsettling development: some Chinese researchers are increasingly concluding that American AI-safety rhetoric is just a form of technological containment. DeepSeek researcher Liu Shengyu’s viral essay argues that frontier AI should be broadly accessible rather than controlled by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI (and yes, he mentions Hitler). In short, American AI safety rhetoric is backfiring in China. Why it matters: If Chinese AI researchers interpret American safety arguments through the lens of anti-China containment, genuine US-China cooperation becomes harder, just as increasingly capable AI makes cooperation more important. items.title: The Spice Trader vs. the Tariffs
items.content: ChinaTalk’s people-suing-the-US-government-over-tariffs series continues. Last time we brought you the grumpy toymaker . Today we have Ethan Frisch, longtime friend of ChinaTalk and co-founder of Burlap & Barrel , finest purveyor of spices in the land. Co-hosting, as always, is Peter Harrell . We discuss: How an aid worker hauling wild cumin out of Afghanistan in duffel bags built a single-origin spice company, and why Burlap & Barrel chooses farmer-led pricing. What Trump’s tariffs cost small businesses and why they’re suing the government, while the large ones sit on the sidelines. The legal case against Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, arguing against executive overreach. Whether forced labor is a real justification or a pretext for recreating the tariffs the Supreme Court struck down, and how long the appeals will run. Plus, the most underappreciated spices, the virtues of a pre-capitalist trading model, and a call to buy small ! Burlap & Barrel promo code: CHINATALK for a free jar of your choice on a first-time order over $15. Listen now on your favorite podcast app . Where the Tariff Litigation Stands Jordan Schneider: Peter, catch us up from where we left off with the Learning Resources CEO. What have the developments been? Peter Harrell: So why are we talking about tariffs again? Didn’t the Supreme Court rule in February that the tariffs were illegal, so they just went away? That’s what most people would assume. But that is not what happened. After the Supreme Court ruled in February, in a case brought by Learning Resources, an educational toy company, that Trump’s first round of tariffs — imposed last year under IEEPA, an emergency powers statute — were illegal, the administration did not give up on tariffs. Instead, they undertook a two-part set of fallback tariffs. The first were in place for 150 days under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 . Those are now expired, but still being litigated.
